requirements.title: What AI does today in cyber

requirements.title: Modalities

requirements.title: Ways of using AI

requirements.title: Anatomy of an agent

requirements.description: Keeping core skills alive and protecting the junior pipeline

requirements.title: Agent incident playbooks
requirements.description: Writing incident playbooks for three agent scenarios: the agent is wrong (it acted on a false conclusion, closed real alerts, changed the wrong thing); the agent is stopped (its identity expired, the provider is down, it ran out of compute) and its work must continue by hand; the agent is compromised (an attacker steered it through content it read). Plans name who can stop the agent (NCSC)

requirements.title: Ways to stop an agent
requirements.description: The ways to stop an agent and when to use each: revoke its identity or session token so it can no longer call any tool; disable only the tools or connectors it misuses while the rest keeps running; put it in observe-only mode, where it may analyse and recommend but is barred from acting; roll back what it changed using its action log

requirements.title: Investigating a compromised agent
requirements.description: Where the attack comes from: content the agent reads (logs, alerts, tickets, documents, emails, web pages) can carry instructions aimed at it, so the investigator looks for injection in those sources and cuts any that is poisoned. What the agent did: knowing, for each of the bank's agents, which records exist that the agent cannot write to and how to pull them fast (the platform's audit log of tool calls with arguments and times, gateway and network logs, logs of the systems it touched), then building the timeline from them, because a compromised agent's own summary can omit or misstate what it did

requirements.title: Cleaning up
requirements.description: Cleaning up after a manipulated agent: finding the injected content it acted on and removing it from the sources the agent reads; clearing anything it stored in its memory as a result; re-running the same injection against the agent before putting it back in service

requirements.title: Operating without the agent
requirements.description: The manual fallback for what the agent handled (triage queue, enrichment, first response), the staffing to sustain it for days, and the regular drill that proves it still works

requirements.title: Reporting
requirements.description: What regulators expect in an incident report when an agent caused or worsened the incident (DORA, HKMA, MAS), and which evidence to preserve for it

requirements.title: Recording the AI step
requirements.description: Recording any AI step applied to evidence so it can be repeated and defended: the tool, model and version, the exact prompt and settings, the output, and who verified it. The original artefact stays the evidence; AI output is a derived analysis, never a substitute

requirements.title: Forensic readiness for agents
requirements.description: Defining what every agent must log (prompt and response, each tool call with its arguments, data retrieved, memory writes, approvals given), stored where the agent cannot alter it, time-synchronised and integrity-protected, retained long enough for an investigation (vendors default to 7 to 30 days), and tested by reconstructing a past incident from it

requirements.title: Investigating an agent as suspect
requirements.description: Rebuilding the agent's actions from its traces, finding the input that steered it, and attributing each action to the human it acted for or to the attacker

requirements.title: AI attack classes
requirements.description: Direct prompt injection; indirect injection through content the agent reads (documents, web pages, tool results, emails); jailbreaks and guardrail evasion; data exfiltration through the agent's own tools; making the agent exceed its intended authority; tool poisoning (a malicious tool description) and rug pulls (a tool that changes after it was approved)

requirements.title: Applying a structured testing method
requirements.description: Apply a structured method to test an AI system or agent: define the scope and attack surface, choose relevant attack cases, execute repeatable tests, record evidence and report findings. Use suitable guidance such as the OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, the CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide or MITRE ATLAS; familiarity with every named publication is not required.

requirements.title: Attacks across agents
requirements.description: Compromising one agent to steer others, injecting into an orchestrator's plan, tampering with messages between agents

requirements.title: Attacks on model and platform
requirements.description: Extracting the model or its instructions, poisoning the agent's memory, escaping the sandbox, timing side channels

requirements.title: Automated red-team programme
requirements.description: Building and running automated red-team harnesses (PyRIT-class tooling) and a continuous programme that re-tests every agent when its model, tools or prompts change

requirements.title: Containment before a run
requirements.description: A network segment from which the agent can reach only in-scope targets; egress allow-lists verified by test, not assumed; a fresh sandbox per run; credentials scoped to the engagement and expiring with it

requirements.title: Monitoring during a run
requirements.description: Watching the agent's actions out of band (not its reports); a named person with the authority and the means to kill the run within minutes; the triggers for doing so (an action outside scope, contact with a third party, a credential used elsewhere)

requirements.title: Escape patterns
requirements.description: The escape patterns seen in practice: attacking something else when the assigned target proves impossible, reading an ambiguous message as approval, creating accounts or identities, carrying on after the window closes, contacting real people

requirements.title: Trajectory-level validation
requirements.description: Validating findings from the transcript, not the summary: check that the evidence the agent cites exists (a 'successful login' that was a redirect, credentials that do not work), reproduce the exploit by hand before reporting, and treat the agent's self-assessment as untrusted

requirements.title: Collateral findings
requirements.description: A disclosure lane for what to do when the agent finds something outside the engagement

requirements.title: Discovery
requirements.description: Finding every MCP server and agent connector in the estate, including those developers run on their own workstations, by searching configuration files and by recognising the MCP protocol in network traffic

requirements.title: Inventory
requirements.description: For each agent and tool server: its owner, version, the tools it exposes, the permissions it holds, the systems it reaches, and the guardrails around it

requirements.title: Verifying approved components and detecting changes
requirements.description: Verify that an agent uses the approved versions of its tools, Skills and connectors, detect changes to their code or descriptions, and require review before changed components are trusted. Use suitable integrity and change-control mechanisms, such as version pinning, signatures or hashes; a particular hashing implementation is not required.

requirements.title: Scanning
requirements.description: Running MCP and Skill scanners in the build pipeline and on a schedule for tool poisoning, instructions hidden in tool descriptions, servers exposed without authentication and credentials stored in plain text

requirements.title: AI bill of materials
requirements.description: A bill of materials for AI components: which models, tools and Skills a system uses and where each came from

requirements.title: Vetting third parties
requirements.description: Vetting third-party Skills and connectors before they are allowed in

requirements.title: Why set-up is the skill
requirements.description: The same model finds under a tenth or over half of the vulnerabilities in a codebase depending on how it is given context and driven, and filters a third or almost all of a static analyser's false positives for the same reason

requirements.title: Giving the model context
requirements.description: Supplying the functions a target calls, type definitions, the data-flow path to the input and build information, using static and dynamic analysis tools to supply that context automatically

requirements.title: Framework, model and method
requirements.description: Choosing the agent framework and the model for the task, and driving the model through a structured method rather than letting it explore freely

requirements.title: Confirming before reporting
requirements.description: A proof of vulnerability (an input or exploit that demonstrates it in a sandbox), the same test against the patched and unpatched versions, and several runs with a majority verdict

requirements.title: Reliability by vulnerability class
requirements.description: Which classes models find well (memory safety, anything a fuzzer can reach) and which they over-report (documented behaviour reported as a bug, inflated severity, duplicates), and setting thresholds per class

requirements.title: Deduplication and cost
requirements.description: Removing duplicates (by stack trace or sanitiser signature) and keeping cost under control at scale

requirements.title: Measuring the harness
requirements.description: Measuring the harness on a corpus of known vulnerabilities before trusting it

requirements.title: Classifying agent actions
requirements.description: For each action an agent can take in a process (a payment, a data deletion, an email to a client, a firewall change), rating its impact and whether it can be undone, and assigning a tier: autonomous, autonomous with logging, human approval, two-person approval, prohibited

requirements.title: Enforcement outside the model
requirements.description: An authorisation point between the agent's plan and its execution that checks every action against its tier and the agent's permissions, so the decision never depends on the model obeying its instructions

requirements.title: The stop mechanism
requirements.description: No standard defines a kill switch, so it is designed as a set of levers (interrupt the task, revoke credentials, cut tool access, quarantine the agent, roll back its changes), each with who may trigger it, how fast it takes effect and how it is tested

requirements.title: The audit trail
requirements.description: What is recorded (reasoning artefacts, each tool call with its arguments, data accessed, messages between agents, approvals), where (a store the agent cannot write to), for how long, and how each action is tied to the person the agent acted for

requirements.title: The oversight interface
requirements.description: How an approval request is shown so a person can judge it (what will happen, in plain language, with the risk and the agent's confidence), limiting the volume of requests so approvers do not click through them, and what overseers must be trained on

requirements.title: Reference architectures
requirements.description: Reference architectures for the bank's agent platforms and how the above is implemented on each

requirements.title: Agent control catalogue
requirements.description: The control catalogue for agents and how to test each control: a distinct identity and permissions per agent, tool allow-lists, logging that the agent cannot alter, approval gates for high-impact actions, change control on prompts, tools and models

requirements.title: Assuring assurance's own AI
requirements.description: Documenting, validating and monitoring the AI used to produce assessments and gather evidence
requirements.coreCondition: When assurance work itself uses AI

requirements.title: Registering an agent
requirements.description: Its own identity (never a shared or human credential), a human sponsor recorded in the directory who is accountable for it, a stated purpose and a declared list of what it may do

requirements.title: Delegated authority
requirements.description: Issuing and reading tokens in which the subject is the person and the actor is the agent (token exchange, on-behalf-of flows), with the person's consent recorded, and what the agent may then do in that person's name

requirements.title: Connector and MCP scopes
requirements.description: Reading what a scope actually permits in the bank's applications and tool servers, granting the minimum, and reviewing grants

requirements.title: Just-in-time access
requirements.description: Privilege granted for a task and a time window with no standing privilege, and the conditions that require a human to approve the grant

requirements.title: Short-lived sub-agents
requirements.description: Identities that exist for seconds, with a time to live and no more rights than the parent

requirements.title: Recertification
requirements.description: Quarterly for agents and monthly for high-privilege ones, with de-provisioning triggered when the sponsor leaves or the purpose lapses

requirements.title: Revocation drills
requirements.description: Revoking an agent's identity and its live sessions within minutes, and verifying that it worked

requirements.title: Integration with IGA, PAM, SIEM
requirements.description: Integrating the agent authorisation point with identity governance, privileged access and the SIEM: registration, scoped issuance, just-in-time grants, recertification and revocation signals flowing between them

requirements.title: Privileged access and break-glass
requirements.description: Privileged access and break-glass for agents inside the existing privileged-access model

requirements.title: Audit trail and standards
requirements.description: The audit trail regulators ask for (which agent, on whose behalf, which tools, what data, what reasoning) and the standards still being written (IETF agent identity, OpenID AuthZEN, MCP authorisation), so the design does not lock into one vendor's delegation model

requirements.title: Overview of AI security risks
requirements.description: Recognise the main categories of security risk affecting AI systems and agents, informed by OWASP's LLM and agentic risk frameworks: instruction manipulation, sensitive-information disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive permissions or actions, compromised components or information sources, and service disruption or uncontrolled resource consumption. Explain a simple example of each and identify an appropriate precaution or escalation route. Foundation awareness does not require threat modelling or memorising framework identifiers.

courses.title: SEC545: GenAI and LLM Application Security (GIAC GAIPS)
courses.description: Advanced defensive course on securing GenAI, LLM and agentic applications: RAG and vector databases, fine-tuning, LangChain, agents and agent protocols (MCP, A2A, ACP), MCP/OAuth attacks including token leakage, memory poisoning and rug pulls, hosting options, MLSecOps (model signing and scanning) and threat modelling with MAESTRO and the OWASP agentic (ASI) taxonomy. Delivered through 20 hands-on labs (e.g. 'Attacking MCP Infrastructure 1/2', 'Compromising LLM Supply Chain', 'Threat Modeling with MAESTRO') and a CTF; maps to GIAC GAIPS.

courses.title: SEC411: AI Security Principles and Practices: GenAI and LLM Defense
courses.description: Intermediate defensive course in three sections (KNOW, DEFEND, DEPLOY) covering LLM architecture and tokenisation risks, threat modelling with MITRE ATLAS, AI supply chain and poisoning, OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, prompt injection and jailbreaking, RAG security, agentic system security (permission models, tool validation, agent control), MCP security, and detection and incident response for prompt, retrieval, tool and memory attacks. Practice is through five labs (LLM Basics, Tokenizer Security Explorer, Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses, RAG Security, MCP Protocol Security) with 125+ lab tasks; no prior AI experience required.

courses.title: SEC495: Leveraging LLMs — Building & Securing RAG, Contextual RAG and Agentic RAG
courses.description: Short hands-on course that builds a self-hosted LLM system with Ollama, then a RAG, contextual RAG and agentic RAG backend, covering embeddings and vector stores, local hosting, reducing hallucinations and cost, attribution, ACL enforcement inside a RAG and defending against prompt injection. One section with five labs (embeddings, Ollama, RAG, 'RAG: Attribution & Security', 'Agentic RAG'); requires intermediate Python.

courses.title: SEC535: Offensive AI — Attack Tools and Techniques (GIAC GOAA)
courses.description: Intermediate offensive course on how attackers use AI across the attack lifecycle: AI-assisted OSINT and reconnaissance, web exploitation, AI-generated phishing, voice and video deepfakes, AI-assisted patch diffing, AI-written and agentic malware, and AI-driven control evasion. Taught through labs such as 'Building PhishGPT', 'ElevenLabs Voice Cloning', vishing and phishing mini-ranges and malware-writing labs, with a capstone CTF; maps to GIAC GOAA.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N1 Partial 56%; N2 Partial 38%; N3 Weak 5%; N5 Partial 61%; N6 Weak 17%; N10 Weak 12% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): SEC535 outline includes model capabilities, decision loops, custom assistants and multimodal deepfakes. Anomalous model behaviour is mentioned; safe agent operation is not the course's purpose. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.description: Intermediate penetration-testing course on attacking AI systems: prompt injection (direct and indirect), memory and RAG poisoning, multimodal evasion, jailbreak chains and guardrail/classifier evasion, exposed AI infrastructure, timing side channels, API authorisation flaws, model weight extraction, alignment and sycophancy probes, sandbox escape, multi-agent attacks and MCP exploitation. R3.1 is scored at Expert because the multi-agent, model-extraction and side-channel labs are specialist content.

courses.description: Six-day bundle of SEC535 (days 1-3: AI for recon, exploitation, phishing, deepfakes and malware) and SEC536 (days 4-6: penetration testing LLMs, RAG, agents, multi-agent systems and MCP servers). courses.title: SEC598: AI and Security Automation for Red, Blue and Purple Teams (GIAC GASAE)
courses.description: Intermediate automation course combining detection-as-code, SOAR (Tines), IaC (Terraform, Ansible), cloud security automation in Azure and AWS, adversary emulation (Atomic, Caldera) and GenAI: LLM-written and LLM-tested detections, RAG-based investigation agents, Bedrock and Azure AI Foundry workflows, CrewAI red-team agents and autonomous/multi-agent SOC agents. 25 labs in a simulated hybrid enterprise plus a capstone; maps to GIAC GASAE. Human-in-the-loop controls are mentioned once; agent oversight, guardrails, MCP and evaluation are not covered.

courses.title: SEC543: AI-Assisted Source Code Analysis and Exploitation for Pen Testers
courses.description: Two-day course on using CLI AI coding agents for source-code review in penetration tests: AI failure modes and verification discipline, secure agent workspace configuration, repository mapping, high-fidelity context extraction, AI-guided logic-flaw hunting, custom tool and exploit generation, isolating vulnerable components in a minimal harness and producing validated, reproducible findings. Ten labs (e.g. 'The Alignment Gap', 'High-Fidelity Context Extraction', 'Component Isolation', 'The Crash and Report').

courses.title: FOR563: Applied AI for DFIR — Leveraging Local LLMs
courses.description: One-day DFIR course on running local LLMs so case data stays private: model setup and local hosting, parameter tuning, natural-language querying of logs, JSON, mobile data and databases, building DFIR-focused agents and basic fine-tuning. Four labs; the author stresses 'trust but verify' and model limitations, but evidence integrity and documenting AI use on evidence are not covered.

courses.description: Leadership course; days 1-2 cover AI: the AI security business case and Shadow AI, NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act and ISO 42001 with cross-framework mapping, CAIO role, governance committees, AI registries and approval workflows, human oversight models (HITL, HOTL, HIC) and their failure modes (complacency, fatigue, atrophy), third-party risk, US/EU/APAC regulation, agentic AI governance, OWASP LLM Top 10 including excessive agency, AI-powered phishing and deepfakes, MITRE ATLAS and AI-SOC investment. courses.title: AI for Cybersecurity
courses.description: 3h foundational course on AI cybersecurity applications, lifecycle, attacks, basic mitigations and threat tools. Public page lists three learning outcomes, video/text, case-study activities and an assessment. No prerequisites; 3 CPEs and validation of completion, with 60-day access. Detailed attack taxonomy and case exercises are not published.

No independent skill credit inferred from the assessment alone. Included in TR-014; do not double count.

courses.title: Securing AI Strategy Workshop
courses.description: Two-day facilitator-led ISC2 workshop delivered by Training Camp. Day 1 covers AI fundamentals (narrow, generative, agentic AI, LLMs), AI maturity assessment, banking and other industry use, the AI lifecycle and roles, Shadow AI, third-party models and vendor due diligence. Day 2 covers NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS, AI attacks and mitigations, data governance, model access controls and output validation, secure deployment of LLM apps and agents, and measuring and reporting AI risk. Practice is through case studies, an AI-use inventory exercise and a capstone AI security roadmap; the listing hides 12 further topics per day.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Two-day facilitator-led ISC2 workshop delivered by Training Camp. Day 1 covers AI fundamentals (narrow, generative, agentic AI, LLMs), AI maturity assessment, banking and other industry use, the AI lifecycle and roles, Shadow AI, third-party models and vendor due diligence. Day 2 covers NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS, AI attacks and mitigations, data governance, model access controls and output validation, secure deployment of LLM apps and agents, and measuring and reporting AI risk. Practice is through case studies, an AI-use inventory exercise and a capstone AI security roadmap; the listing hides 12 further topics per day.

courses.title: AAISM — Advanced in AI Security Management (requires CISM/CISSP)
courses.description: Exam-only credential for holders of CISM or CISSP, built on a three-domain outline: AI Governance and Program Management (31%), AI Risk Management (31%) and AI Technologies and Controls (38%), with 22 task statements. It covers AI security policy, AI risk assessment with thresholds and treatment, vendor and supply-chain management, AI asset inventory, AI incident handling and security architecture at management level; preparation is via the official review manual and question database, with no labs. Neither the outline nor the manual description mentions agents, agentic AI, prompt injection, OWASP or MITRE ATLAS.

courses.title: AI Fundamentals Certificate
courses.description: Entry-level certificate for students and people new to IT, with a 2-hour online multiple-choice exam split between AI Concepts and AI Implementations. Stated topics are AI principles, machine learning models, robotic process automation, statistical sampling and modelling, regression, and a general 'AI associated risks and ethical requirements' area; the lab package covers ML models, security implementations of AI and RPA. There is no mention of generative AI, LLMs, agents, hallucination or prompt injection.

courses.title: AAISM Certification Prep
courses.description: Two-day instructor-led exam-prep course for the ISACA AAISM exam (voucher, review question database and coaching included; CISM or CISSP required to certify). The detailed outline follows the three AAISM domains and adds topics such as AI asset inventory and model cards, risk thresholds and treatment, AI-specific incident playbooks and break-glass policies, vendor due diligence and provider-versus-deployer accountability, red teaming and AI threats including deepfakes and AI agents, and human-in-the-loop controls. It is lecture and exam-question based; no labs are mentioned.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N3 Weak 5%; N4 Partial 52%; N5 Partial 33%; N7 Weak 7%; N13 Partial 56%; N14 Weak 10% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Two-day instructor-led exam-prep course for the ISACA AAISM exam (voucher, review question database and coaching included; CISM or CISSP required to certify). The detailed outline follows the three AAISM domains and adds topics such as AI asset inventory and model cards, risk thresholds and treatment, AI-specific incident playbooks and break-glass policies, vendor due diligence and provider-versus-deployer accountability, red teaming and AI threats including deepfakes and AI agents, and human-in-the-loop controls. It is lecture and exam-question based; no labs are mentioned.

courses.title: SecAI+ (CY0-001)
courses.description: Vendor-neutral certification for security staff with 3-4 years in IT, covering basic AI concepts for cyber (17%), securing AI systems (40%), AI-assisted security (24%) and AI GRC (19%). The detailed objectives cover AI threat modelling with the OWASP LLM/ML Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS, guardrails and gateway controls, model/data/agent access control, prompt and log monitoring, a long list of attacks (prompt injection, jailbreaks, excessive agency, insecure plug-ins, overreliance), AI-enabled attacks including deepfakes, AI tools for security tasks (including MCP servers and AI agents), and governance (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, shadow AI). The exam includes performance-based items and CompTIA sells separate virtual labs; supervising agents is touched only via human oversight and excessive agency.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: V13: zero taught coverage on all 140 outcomes. Exam scope is not teaching.
courses.limitations: Exam-only record with optional preparation purchased separately. All teaching scores are zero, including corrected N5.8. courses.title: C|OASP — Certified Offensive AI Security Professional
courses.description: Offensive AI security course and certification for penetration testers and red teamers, in 10 modules: methodology mapped to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP LLM/ML/Agentic Top 10, AI reconnaissance, scanning and fuzzing, prompt injection and LLM app attacks, adversarial ML and model extraction, data/pipeline poisoning, agentic AI and model-to-model attacks (excessive agency, cross-LLM, orchestration-layer attacks), infrastructure and supply-chain attacks, testing and hardening, and AI incident response. It includes 30 labs (e.g. Cross-LLM Attacks, RAG Poisoning, model extraction) and tools such as PyRIT and Garak; the exam includes practical challenges. Each module is only 45-70 minutes, so depth per topic is limited.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Weak 10%; N3 Weak 10%; N4 Weak 10%; N5 Weak 24%; N8 Weak 7%; N12 Weak 30%; R1.1 Weak 6%; R3.1 Partial 67% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Offensive AI security course and certification for penetration testers and red teamers, in 10 modules: methodology mapped to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP LLM/ML/Agentic Top 10, AI reconnaissance, scanning and fuzzing, prompt injection and LLM app attacks, adversarial ML and model extraction, data/pipeline poisoning, agentic AI and model-to-model attacks (excessive agency, cross-LLM, orchestration-layer attacks), infrastructure and supply-chain attacks, testing and hardening, and AI incident response. It includes 30 labs (e.g. Cross-LLM Attacks, RAG Poisoning, model extraction) and tools such as PyRIT and Garak; the exam includes practical challenges. Each module is only 45-70 minutes, so depth per topic is limited.

courses.title: CEH v13 (AI-integrated)
courses.description: Classic 20-module ethical hacking course (reconnaissance through cryptography) with 221 labs, now with 'AI-integrated' labs in ten modules where learners use AI tools such as ShellGPT and ChatGPT-based tools for OSINT, scanning, vulnerability analysis, exploitation, social engineering and web attacks. It mentions AI-based malware and AI-driven impersonation; there is no dedicated module on attacking LLMs or agents, and no coverage of agents, prompt injection or MITRE ATLAS.

courses.title: C|RAGE — Certified Responsible AI Governance & Ethics
courses.description: Governance and ethics certification for GRC, privacy, audit and security professionals, with no technical AI background required. Eleven modules of 45-70 minutes cover AI foundations, ethics and responsible AI, strategy, governance operating models and human oversight, regulatory compliance (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001), AI risk and threat management, third-party AI and supply chain, security architecture, privacy and trust, AI incident response, and AI assurance, testing and audit. No labs are listed, and agents and agentic AI are not covered.

courses.title: C|AIPM — Certified AI Program Manager
courses.description: Business-focused programme-management certification on taking AI from pilot to enterprise deployment, aimed at programme managers, strategists and IT/security staff with two or more years' experience. Ten modules cover AI fundamentals (agents mentioned only as a type of AI), readiness and maturity, use-case prioritisation and ROI, roadmaps and operating models, change management (ADKAR, Kotter) and AI literacy programmes, platforms and vendors, governance and ethics, pilots and scaling, measuring adoption and value, and sustaining transformation. It uses structured exercises and templates rather than labs.

Agents, hallucination and prompt injection are not mentioned, and the page's two curriculum sections are inconsistent.

courses.title: AI-300 Advanced AI Red Teaming (OSAI+)
courses.description: Advanced (300-level) AI red-teaming course for experienced pentesters and red teamers, with 11 modules: AI red-teaming intro, reconnaissance, attacking AI agents (prompt instructions, memory), attacking multi-agent systems and A2A protocols, RAG poisoning, embedding attacks, attacking MCP and tool surfaces to escalate privileges, AI supply chain, AI infrastructure, threat modelling of AI targets, and a capstone red-team engagement. Labs simulate enterprise AI architectures (LLMs, vector databases, multi-agent and orchestration frameworks), and the certification is a 24-hour hands-on exam. The syllabus has one-line module descriptions and does not mention OWASP, MITRE ATLAS or automated red-team tooling.

courses.description: Self-paced OffSec learning path on attacking LLM applications. OffSec's blog describes four areas (LLM foundations including tokenisation and embeddings, enumeration of LLM apps, attack techniques such as prompt injection, jailbreaking, improper output handling, supply-chain manipulation and abuse of excessive agent permissions, and reporting business impact), with sandboxed labs using Open WebUI, Ollama and LangChain agents. The module list, hours and lab titles could not be verified because the course page did not render.

courses.title: AIGP — AI Governance Professional (BoK v2.1)
courses.description: IAPP governance certification organised in four domains: foundations of AI governance, laws, standards and frameworks applied to AI (privacy law, other laws, AI-specific laws, industry standards), governing AI development, and governing AI deployment and use (deployment decision, impact assessment, ongoing monitoring). The Feb 2025 BoK added AI characteristics such as autonomy, developer/deployer/user distinctions and impact assessments. The detailed BoK v2.1 PDF could not be retrieved, so the 'agentic architectures added' claim in the draft could not be confirmed; the Feb 2026 study guide does not mention agents, third-party AI, inventory or human oversight.

courses.title: TAISE — Trusted AI Safety Expert
courses.description: CSA certificate (training plus exam bundle, USD 795) with ten modules: intro to AI, generative AI architecture, use cases, ethics and explainability, model lifecycle and threat taxonomy, governance/risk/compliance, AI security and safety, cloud and AI security, data security and privacy, and continuous adaptation. It is built around CSA's AI Controls Matrix, NIST AI RMF and ISO standards, with a prompt library instead of labs. Only module titles were available; agents are not covered in the current certificate (a separate agentic TAISE track exists only as a March 2026 draft white paper).

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). Security/privacy risks, safety constraints or controls are named in the retained public syllabus, but a coherent explanation of the revised security-risk overview is not established. Reviewed syllabus: CSA certificate (training plus exam bundle, USD 795) with ten modules: intro to AI, generative AI architecture, use cases, ethics and explainability, model lifecycle and threat taxonomy, governance/risk/compliance, AI security and safety, cloud and AI security, data security and privacy, and continuous adaptation. It is built around CSA's AI Controls Matrix, NIST AI RMF and ISO standards, with a prompt library instead of labs. Only module titles were available; agents are not covered in the current certificate (a separate agentic TAISE track exists only as a March 2026 draft white paper).

courses.title: ISO/IEC 42001 Lead Implementer
courses.description: Five-day PECB course on planning, implementing, monitoring and improving an AI management system (AIMS) to ISO/IEC 42001 using PECB's IMS2 methodology, ending in a 3-hour certification exam. Day-level agenda covers context and scope, AI policy, AI risk management, Statement of Applicability, control selection and implementation, documented information, internal audit, management review and certification-audit preparation. Practice is essay-type exercises and scenario quizzes; there are no technical labs and nothing specific to agents.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N4 Weak 5%; N13 Partial 39%; N14 Weak 5% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): AIMS course addresses management-system roles and standard compliance, not the bank's AI rules or complete agent accountability. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.title: CMCPSE — Certified MCP Security Expert
courses.description: Self-paced hands-on certification on Model Context Protocol security: MCP architecture and building a server, MCP attack primitives (tool poisoning, injection via tool responses, impersonation, rug pulls, cross-server escalation, confused deputy), STRIDE/ATLAS threat modelling, hardening (OAuth scopes, RBAC, secrets vault, tool-invocation logging, AI firewall), DevSecOps gates and supply chain (SBOM, signing, vetting third-party servers). Each chapter has labs; the exam is five practical challenges in 6 hours plus a report.

courses.title: Generative AI Security
courses.description: One-day instructor-led Pluralsight professional-services course (beginner) for developers, data engineers and security engineers: GenAI risks (model theft, data leakage, adversarial manipulation, deepfakes), data privacy and differential privacy, adversarial attacks and defences including prompt injection, and secure integration of GenAI into applications. Delivery is described as hands-on and project-focused on the client's own stack, but no labs are listed; nothing on agents.

courses.title: AI for Cybersecurity Specialization
courses.description: Three-course Johns Hopkins specialization on classical machine learning for security: ML spam/phishing classification, biometric authentication, malware and network anomaly detection (clustering, decision trees, HMM), fraud detection, GANs and black/white-box adversarial attacks. Graded coding projects build IoT botnet and metamorphic malware detectors in Jupyter. Course pages give learning outcomes, not module titles, and there is no LLM, generative AI or agent content.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N1 Partial 33%; N2 Weak 5%; N5 Weak 11%; N9 Weak 13%; N11 Weak 6% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Classical ML projects use validation and known datasets, but do not teach an agent-specific domain evaluation system. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.title: Generative AI for Cybersecurity Professionals
courses.description: IBM three-course series: a GenAI introduction, prompt engineering basics (zero/few-shot, watsonx Prompt Lab), and 'Boost your cybersecurity career', which covers GenAI for SOC work (incident triage, log analysis, threat hunting, vulnerability management, SIEM/UEBA, report summarisation and playbooks), GenAI risks and ethics, in short videos with about six 20-30 minute guided labs, quizzes and a final project. Full module and lecture list seen only for the third course; nothing on agents.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N1 Partial 67%; N4 Weak 11%; N5 Weak 22%; N6 Partial 33% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Cybersecurity career module includes risks and ethics; guided labs do not establish agent supervision or code-analysis harness design. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

Per the delivery partner's curriculum article, it runs four modules: AI-enabled cybercrime (deepfakes, voice cloning, AI phishing), governance with MITRE ATLAS, OWASP LLM Top 10 and NIST AI RMF (policy drafting, AI risk assessments), AI abuse, agents and autonomous cyber operations, and shadow AI, human risk and awareness. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Live online MIT xPRO programme, delivered with Emeritus, for CISOs and senior risk and IT leaders. Per the delivery partner's curriculum article, it runs four modules: AI-enabled cybercrime (deepfakes, voice cloning, AI phishing), governance with MITRE ATLAS, OWASP LLM Top 10 and NIST AI RMF (policy drafting, AI risk assessments), AI abuse, agents and autonomous cyber operations, and shadow AI, human risk and awareness. Exercises are case studies, policy drafting, risk assessments, simulations and a capstone; the official pages give no week-level syllabus.

courses.title: AI Executive Academy
courses.description: Two-week on-campus MIT Sloan / Schwarzman College programme for senior executives: AI overview, ML and data, problem formulation and AI workflows/automation, NLP, multi-modal AI, strategy and innovation, the human element, ethics and governance, and adapting to radical AI advances, ending with capstone presentations. Only session titles are published; it is general business AI education with no cyber or agent-supervision content. Tuition is about USD 24,500.

courses.title: AI and Cybersecurity (Blended)
courses.description: NUS-ISS course for cybersecurity and cyber-risk professionals with foundational ML knowledge. The six listed topics are an overview, threat modelling AI systems, exploiting vulnerabilities in ML-based AI systems, engineering mitigations, harnessing AI for cyber defence, and AI-powered attacks and mitigations. Delivered through Zoom sessions, group activities and an assessment; no labs or lecture-level detail are published, and it is framed around ML systems rather than agents.

courses.title: AI Red Teamer job-role path
courses.description: Hard-rated 12-module path built with Google and aligned to SAIF: ML fundamentals, introduction to red teaming AI (OWASP ML and LLM Top 10, SAIF), prompt injection (direct, indirect, jailbreaks), LLM output attacks, data poisoning, application and system attacks including MCP (vulnerable and malicious MCP servers), adversarial evasion, privacy attacks and an AI Defense module on guardrails. Each module ends with a hands-on skills assessment. Most of the path is classic ML/LLM attack content; agent-specific and multi-agent attacks are thin.

courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Path modules include supply-chain attacks and malicious MCP servers. Generic ML model building is not agent engineering or operator evaluation. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

Reviewed syllabus: Hard-rated 12-module path built with Google and aligned to SAIF: ML fundamentals, introduction to red teaming AI (OWASP ML and LLM Top 10, SAIF), prompt injection (direct, indirect, jailbreaks), LLM output attacks, data poisoning, application and system attacks including MCP (vulnerable and malicious MCP servers), adversarial evasion, privacy attacks and an AI Defense module on guardrails. courses.title: HTB COAE — Certified Offensive AI Expert
courses.description: A hands-on certification exam launched April 2026: candidates run a full AI offensive assessment of a simulated corporate environment over seven days. It assesses the content of the AI Red Teamer path (TR-049): adversarial ML, data poisoning, prompt injection and jailbreaking, LLM output abuse, AI application and system security, privacy and defence, aligned to SAIF and the OWASP ML, LLM and Agentic Top 10s. It is an assessment, not a course; the exam scenario details are not public.

courses.title: HTB AI Range
courses.description: A controlled cyber range, launched December 2025, for testing and benchmarking autonomous AI security agents side by side with human operators on thousands of offensive and defensive targets mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, NIST/NICE and OWASP Top 10. An Enterprise Edition (Oct 2026) lets organisations test their own agents against the tasks they will do. Sources describe a benchmarking platform; no curriculum, lessons or exercises that teach people are published.

courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Benchmarking infrastructure with no published learner curriculum; resource availability is not teaching coverage. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.title: AI Security path + AI1 certification
courses.description: Intermediate path of 5 modules and 25 hands-on rooms launched April 2026, mapped to the OWASP LLM Top 10: AI fundamentals (incl. AI threats and AI forensics), securing AI systems (LLM security, AI threat modelling, reconnaissance, threat-modelling assessment), prompt security (injection, jailbreaking, prompt defence, challenge rooms), AI supply chain security and data poisoning/RAG security. The AI1 certification tests 13 attack-and-defend scenarios; its format is not published. No agent, MCP or tool-use content is listed.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N3 Weak 14%; N4 Weak 19%; N5 Weak 17%; N12 Weak 22%; R1.2 Weak 11%; R3.1 Partial 50% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): AI forensics is only named; supply-chain security is a taught module. No agent forensic readiness or evidence-preservation method is evidenced. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.title: AI Advantage: Elevating Cyber Defense
courses.description: An 8-hour on-demand Mandiant Academy track for front-line defenders and CTI analysts in three courses: introduction to AI (terminology, Google GenAI tools, risks, responsible use, prompting), optimising common intelligence tasks (research, writing, summarising) and AI across collection, organisation and analysis (IOC analysis, preliminary malware analysis, vulnerability identification, repeatable processes with agents). Delivery is by demonstration with Gemini, NotebookLM and Colab; no labs are listed. Costs USD 2,000.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N1 Partial 56%; N6 Weak 29%; N14 Weak 5% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Defender workflow examples and responsible-use introduction; demonstrations do not evidence complete oversight practice. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Twelve self-hosted challenges (Docker plus an Azure OpenAI or OpenAI key) from Microsoft's Black Hat USA 2024 'AI Red Teaming in Practice' course: credential exfiltration by direct prompt injection, metaprompt secret extraction, Crescendo multi-turn jailbreaks with and without guardrails, and indirect prompt injection through a mock web page, at easy to hard levels. PyRIT notebooks are provided for several labs. Practice only; no teaching material or agent/tool scenarios.

courses.title: PyRIT documentation and cookbooks
courses.description: Documentation for Microsoft's open-source Python Risk Identification Tool: targets (OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic, Google, HTTP, Playwright web apps), converters, scorers (true/false, Likert, custom), single-turn, multi-turn (Crescendo, TAP, Skeleton Key) and compound attacks, GCG suffixes, benchmarks, a scenario framework, memory, plus workflows such as cross-domain prompt injection (XPIA) against a tool-using summarisation agent and a RAG recruiter. Runnable notebooks, but it is tool documentation, not a course.

courses.title: Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Agentic AI Systems v2.0
courses.description: Microsoft AI Red Team's 16-page update of its agentic failure-mode taxonomy, based on a year of red-team engagements. It adds seven failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP/plugin abuse incl. tool description poisoning, capability disclosure) and reports human-in-the-loop bypass via consent fatigue as the most exploited. The mitigations section covers supply-chain controls, zero-trust inter-agent identity, consent architecture hardening (tiered approvals by reversibility, decomposed actions, approval-rate monitoring), session hardening and output filtering, and maps to OWASP, CSA, MITRE and NIST. Reading only; no exercises.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Microsoft AI Red Team's 16-page update of its agentic failure-mode taxonomy, based on a year of red-team engagements. It adds seven failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP/plugin abuse incl. tool description poisoning, capability disclosure) and reports human-in-the-loop bypass via consent fatigue as the most exploited. The mitigations section covers supply-chain controls, zero-trust inter-agent identity, consent architecture hardening (tiered approvals by reversibility, decomposed actions, approval-rate monitoring), session hardening and output filtering, and maps to OWASP, CSA, MITRE and NIST. Reading only; no exercises.

courses.description: Cloud Adoption Framework page setting a governance and security baseline for agents: accountability aligned to existing governance owners, a single agent registry (owner, purpose, platform, access scope) using Agent 365 or Entra Agent ID, distinct agent identities, allow/block lists for tools and MCP servers, monitoring and cost tracking, data privacy, residency and retention, least privilege, red teaming before production, SOC routing and an incident plan to disable an agent. courses.title: Secure AI Framework (SAIF) + Risk Map
courses.description: Google's framework site: an interactive SAIF Map of AI development components, 15 named risks (data poisoning, model source tampering, prompt injection, sensitive data disclosure, insecure integrated component, rogue actions, etc.) each linked to named controls, a 'Focus on Agents' page and an Agent Risk Self Assessment questionnaire. The agents page covers rogue actions and data disclosure through tools, and controls such as least-privilege agent permissions, user approval of consequential actions, agent observability, output sanitisation and input filtering. Reading and a self-assessment only; no exercises.

courses.title: AI Technical Practitioner (AITECH)
courses.description: Vendor-neutral-in-content Cisco certification for technical IT staff: a 13-lesson course (GenAI ecosystem, prompt engineering, security and privacy fundamentals, debugging AI outputs, APIs, AI in software engineering and data work, fine-tuning vs RAG, workflows and agentic AI) and a 60-minute exam weighted 20% models, 15% prompting (incl. prompt injection types), 15% ethics and security, 10% data, 20% development and workflow automation, 20% agentic AI (design, autonomy, orchestration, MCP primitives, human-in-the-loop). Labs are claimed but not listed. Broad and general-purpose; not cyber-specific.

courses.title: Introduction to AI Vulnerabilities
courses.description: Free 35-minute Cisco U. tutorial, described in a May 2025 Cisco blog, on AI threat vectors (prompt injection, data poisoning, adversarial attacks, model evasion), the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and MITRE ATLAS, with short attack simulations and defences such as monitoring, adversarial testing and model hardening. It is positioned as a lead-in to Cisco AI Defense. Only the blog description was available.

courses.title: garak LLM vulnerability scanner
courses.description: NVIDIA's open-source scanner that probes LLMs for jailbreaks (DAN, GCG suffixes), encoding-based prompt injection, training-data replay, hallucination, malware generation, toxicity and XSS-style exfiltration, using probes, detectors and a harness against many model endpoints, with JSONL reports. Documentation, a research paper and DEF CON slides exist, but no structured training; there are no agent or tool-use probes.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N3 Weak 10%; N4 Weak 5%; N9 Weak 27%; N11 Weak 6%; R3.1 Weak 27% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). Security/privacy risks, safety constraints or controls are named in the retained public syllabus, but a coherent explanation of the revised security-risk overview is not established. Reviewed syllabus: NVIDIA's open-source scanner that probes LLMs for jailbreaks (DAN, GCG suffixes), encoding-based prompt injection, training-data replay, hallucination, malware generation, toxicity and XSS-style exfiltration, using probes, detectors and a harness against many model endpoints, with JSONL reports. Documentation, a research paper and DEF CON slides exist, but no structured training; there are no agent or tool-use probes.
N5.8.change: V11 reassessment; prior v10 score: not assessed

courses.title: AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations (4D: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence)
courses.description: L1 AI-assisted work through Delegation, Description, Discernment and Diligence. 14 lessons, one quiz and a completion badge; published learning estimate 4h. Public lessons include task-allocation exercises, prompt improvement, expert-domain output review and a continuing project with a diligence statement. Generic and transferable, with supporting Foundation concepts.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: V12 review: N2 29% Weak; N3 29% Weak; N4 11% Weak; N6 67% Partial. Current results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: 31 Oct 2026: L1 / N6 primary, Foundation support secondary. The four core N6 outcomes have explicit teaching and practice; the rubric does not require graded labs. Does not complete bank platform/data rules, model/effort choice or memory management. Public lessons reviewed, not a course-completion claim. Supersedes the historical V8 audit for this course.

courses.title: Building effective human–agent teams (beta)
courses.description: Short beta course on Claude Academy (academy.claude.com, not the Skilljar catalogue) for team leads, on moving from single-player AI to multiplayer agents that work as team members. Five lessons cover why multiplayer AI matters, how such agents differ from chatbots, what a strong human-agent team looks like, an organisational checklist, and ways to get started, with four principles: clear roles, a written north star, gradual release and the right information access. Assessment is a quiz; no exercises are listed.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N1 Partial 33%; N2 Weak 14%; N6 Weak 4%; N7 Weak 7%; N13 Weak 6%; N14 Weak 29% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Team roles, gradual release and information boundaries introduce delegation and autonomy; surrounding Academy course advertisements excluded. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.title: Introduction to MCP / MCP: Advanced Topics
courses.description: Two developer courses. The introduction builds an MCP server and client in Python (tools, resources and prompts, the server inspector, a document-management example). The advanced course covers sampling, progress and logging notifications, roots-based file access, JSON message types, the STDIO and StreamableHTTP transports, and stateless scaling. Both are video lessons with code walkthroughs and end in an assessment. Security is limited to roots-based file boundaries, and authorisation is not covered.

courses.title: Agents and Workflows
courses.description: Third course in OpenAI Academy's 'Apply AI at Work' path (launched 12 Jun 2026) for knowledge workers. Per OpenAI's announcement, learners direct agent-assisted work by giving context, defining outputs and boundaries, and reviewing results. They practise running and refining a reusable workflow and decide where human judgment and oversight are needed. It ends with an assessment and a badge. The course page is rendered by script, so the module list and duration could not be seen.

courses.title: Lead AI Adoption (leaders track)
courses.description: The 'Lead AI Adoption' path on OpenAI Academy holds a single course, AI Leadership, for leaders responsible for AI strategy, adoption, change and workforce transformation. Per OpenAI's descriptions, participants complete one AI initiative and draft an initial AI strategy. They link AI to business priorities, assess opportunities, set ownership and governance, and build an adoption roadmap. Risk is not mentioned, and modules and duration are not published on the pages that could be read.

courses.title: Agentic AI
courses.description: Andrew Ng's Coursera course builds agentic workflows in Python from first principles. It covers task decomposition, degrees of autonomy, reflection, tool use (including code execution and MCP), planning and multi-agent patterns, and a module on evals, error analysis, component-level evaluation, and latency and cost. It has 31 videos, 5 quizzes, 3 graded programming labs and 7 ungraded labs.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Partial 38%; N6 Weak 4%; N9 Partial 47%; N10 Partial 42%; N11 Weak 28% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Evaluation/error-analysis module teaches test examples, component diagnosis and performance metrics. It does not validate judges against human labels or aggregate a whole domain's practitioner results. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit. V10 recheck (2026-10-18): Rechecked the five-module agent-design and evaluation syllabus. Retain the existing Coursera offering and its approximately 23-hour estimate; record DeepLearning.AI's 9h55m platform duration separately, since platform time accounting differs. No duplicate offering or score inflation.

courses.title: Red Teaming LLM Applications
courses.cost: Free access advertised at review; Pro graded work/accomplishment; external service costs may apply
courses.description: Short Giskard course with 7 video lessons: an overview of LLM vulnerabilities, manual red teaming, red teaming at scale, using LLMs to red-team LLMs with Giskard's open-source library, and a full red-teaming assessment of chatbot apps, plus a quiz. The page lists no code examples, though it describes manual and automated practice. It targets chatbot and RAG apps, not agents with tools.

courses.title: Evaluating AI Agents
courses.cost: Free access advertised at review; Pro graded work/accomplishment; external service costs may apply
courses.description: Arize AI short course with 15 video lessons and 5 code labs. Learners build an agent with a router, skills and memory, add tracing, then add router and skill evaluations, trajectory evaluations (convergence score), and structured experiments that vary prompts, models or logic. Lessons cover code-based, LLM-as-judge and human-annotation evaluators, improving the LLM judge, and monitoring agents in production.

V10 recheck (2026-10-18): Rechecked five agent/tracing/evaluation labs and judge-improvement/monitoring lessons. Existing scores remain appropriate; explicit validation of judges against a complete human-labelled reference is still not established. Refresh platform time and access metadata.

courses.title: Safe and Reliable AI via Guardrails
courses.cost: Free access advertised at review; Pro graded work/accomplishment; external service costs may apply
courses.description: GuardrailsAI short course by Shreya Rajpal. Using a RAG customer-service chatbot, learners build input and output guards for hallucination (an NLI model), off-topic content, PII leakage and competitor mentions, from scratch and from the GuardrailsAI hub. It has 7 code examples and a quiz. Prompt injection and attacks that evade guardrails are not covered.

Existing scores remain appropriate; no comprehensive adversarial guardrail evaluation is evidenced. Refresh public time and access metadata.

courses.title: A2A: The Agent2Agent Protocol
courses.cost: See membership pricing; Pro graded work/certificate; external service costs may apply
courses.description: Google Cloud and IBM Research short course. Learners wrap agents built with Claude on Vertex AI, Google ADK, LangGraph with MCP, and BeeAI as A2A servers, call them from A2A clients, and orchestrate sequential and hierarchical multi-agent workflows, then deploy on BeeAI Agent Stack. It has 8 code examples and a quiz. Security gets a single 4-minute lesson on extensions and security.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Weak 14%; N10 Weak 25%; N12 Weak 7% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Brief extensions/security lesson mentions protocol security; no full identity or authorisation engineering practice. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit. V10 recheck (2026-10-18): Rechecked A2A server/client, multi-framework orchestration and brief security lesson. Existing requirement scores remain appropriate. Replace the generic directory link and unknown duration with this exact syllabus and its published learning time.

courses.title: AI Agents Course
courses.description: Free self-paced course. Unit 1 covers agent fundamentals: LLMs, messages, tools, the thought-action-observation cycle and ReAct, ending with building a first agent. Unit 2 covers the smolagents, LlamaIndex and LangGraph frameworks (including multi-agent systems), Unit 3 agentic RAG use cases, and Unit 4 a final benchmarked agent assignment with a leaderboard. Bonus units cover function-calling fine-tuning, observability and evaluation (OpenTelemetry tracing, online LLM-as-judge and offline benchmark evaluation, with a notebook), and a games agent. Security is not covered.

Security/privacy risks, safety constraints or controls are named in the retained public syllabus, but a coherent explanation of the revised security-risk overview is not established. Reviewed syllabus: Recorded Berkeley lecture series by Dawn Song and guest speakers from OpenAI, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, Google DeepMind and Sierra. It covers LLM agent foundations, system design, post-training verifiable agents, agent evaluation, multi-agent AI, statistical noise in evals, scientific-discovery agents, lessons from real deployments, embodied agents, and a closing lecture on agentic AI safety and security. Assessment is quizzes plus an article or a project (AgentBeats evaluator 'green agent' and 'white agent'); there are no labs.

courses.title: CS329Z Engineering AI Agents (public materials)
courses.description: Stanford course running in Fall 2026 (Diyi Yang, Michael Ryan, John Yang). Topics are LLMs for builders and context engineering; RAG; tool use and MCP with sandboxes; frameworks (DSPy, LangGraph); agent design patterns; memory and multi-agent systems; optimisation; data from traces; evaluation fundamentals; LLM-as-judge and eval infrastructure; safety (prompt injection, red-teaming, sandboxing, guardrails, human-in-the-loop); and coding agents. As of 13 Oct 2026 only slides for lectures 1-5 are public. There are no public videos, and the homework and project are for enrolled students.

courses.title: Technical AI Safety
courses.description: Free BlueDot Impact cohort course on frontier AI safety research. Six units cover the technical challenge, training safer models (data, RLHF), detecting danger (evaluations and how Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Meta test for safety), interpretability, minimising harm (assuming harm, building defences, breaking the kill chain), and career next steps. Each unit has 2-3 hours of reading plus a facilitated 2-hour discussion; there are no labs.
courses.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Weak 5%; N11 Weak 11%; N12 Weak 4% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Frontier-model alignment, evaluations and defence research are adjacent introductions, not agent operating skills. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

Reviewed syllabus: Free BlueDot Impact cohort course on frontier AI safety research. Six units cover the technical challenge, training safer models (data, RLHF), detecting danger (evaluations and how Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Meta test for safety), interpretability, minimising harm (assuming harm, building defences, breaking the kill chain), and career next steps. Each unit has 2-3 hours of reading plus a facilitated 2-hour discussion; there are no labs.

courses.title: Frontier AI Governance
courses.description: Free BlueDot Impact cohort course on public-policy governance of frontier AI. Six units cover assessing system cards and independent evaluations, mapping institutions and power, comparing governance strategies, stress-testing proposals, a debate on open weights or restraint, and a personal contribution plan, with exercises such as decision-maker briefings and a simulated oversight board. Its FAQ states it is not about corporate compliance or internal AI-use policies.

courses.title: Inspect evaluation framework
courses.description: This is software documentation for a Python evaluation framework, not a course. It covers tasks, datasets, solvers, scorers (text-match and model-graded), running evals across model providers, a ReAct agent, multi-agent handoff, tools including MCP, sandboxing, tool approval, and log analysis. There is a tutorial with annotated examples (a QA benchmark and a capture-the-flag agent task) but no graded exercises, and it assumes Python skills.

courses.title: LLM Top 10 2026
courses.description: A 122-page reference guide that ranks the ten main security risks of LLM applications for 2026: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, supply chain, data and model poisoning, unbounded consumption, misinformation, hidden context exposure, vector and embedding weaknesses, and improper output handling. Each entry gives attack scenarios and mitigations, and the appendices map the risks to ATLAS, the Agentic Top 10, NIST and CWE, and describe an LLM application architecture for threat modelling. It is reading only; there are no exercises.

courses.title: Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
courses.description: A peer-reviewed reference guide to the ten main risks of agentic applications (ASI01-ASI10): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. Each entry has attack scenarios and mitigations. The appendices map the risks to the LLM Top 10, CycloneDX/AIBOM and the Non-Human Identities Top 10, and include an incident tracker. It is reading only.

This is Foundation knowledge credit, not security-design practice or bank-specific evidence. Reviewed syllabus: A peer-reviewed reference guide to the ten main risks of agentic applications (ASI01-ASI10): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. Each entry has attack scenarios and mitigations. The appendices map the risks to the LLM Top 10, CycloneDX/AIBOM and the Non-Human Identities Top 10, and include an incident tracker. It is reading only.

courses.title: Agentic AI — Threats & Mitigations v1.0
courses.description: A threat-model reference for agentic AI with three main parts: an agentic reference architecture (agent layer, LLM, tools/MCP, memory and RAG, multi-agent A2A), a threat taxonomy (T1-T17, including memory poisoning, tool misuse, repudiation, identity spoofing and overwhelming the human in the loop), and a six-step taxonomy navigator. It also has six mitigation playbooks and worked example threat models such as an enterprise copilot. It is reading only, with no exercises.

courses.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
courses.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. Deterministic policy (OPA/Rego, Cedar) runs first, and there are an audit chain, OpenTelemetry/OCSF tracing and an AgBOM inventory. A reference Guardian with Claude Code and OpenCode shims can be run, but there is no tutorial or exercise; the README notes known gaps (unsigned wire, fail-open default).

Reviewed syllabus: A red-teaming methodology guide that covers scope, risks, threat modelling (ATLAS, NIST AI 600-1, STRIDE), strategy, and a four-phase blueprint (model, implementation, system, runtime/human and agentic) with checklists. courses.title: AI Testing Guide v1
courses.description: A testing standard for AI systems with a threat-modelling chapter (mapping OWASP threats to AI architecture components, SAIF-based) and 32 test cases across the application, model, infrastructure and data layers. These include direct and indirect prompt injection, agentic behaviour limits, hallucinations, over-reliance, supply chain tampering and runtime exfiltration. Each test case gives objectives, test payloads, expected output, remediation and tools. It is reading only, with no lab environment.

courses.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Published test cases include expected results, remediation, delegated identity and permission abuse. Reading-only test library, not completed practice. The provider guidance names non-deterministic AI failure as a difference from software testing; this is awareness rather than complete teaching. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

courses.title: FinBot Agentic AI CTF
courses.description: A hosted or self-hostable, intentionally vulnerable vendor-management fintech platform where LLM agents with real tools and MCP servers (FinDrive, FinStripe, FinMail, TaxCalc) handle onboarding, fraud checks, invoices and payments. Players attack it through challenge tiers (recon/system-prompt extraction, policy bypass via goal manipulation, data exfiltration, destructive actions, RCE through tool poisoning and MCP). Challenges are detected automatically, offer hints and are mapped to the OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10s and ATLAS. It is attacker-side practice only: there are no walkthroughs and no defence or detection exercises, and multi-agent and memory-poisoning challenges are still on the roadmap.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: A hosted or self-hostable, intentionally vulnerable vendor-management fintech platform where LLM agents with real tools and MCP servers (FinDrive, FinStripe, FinMail, TaxCalc) handle onboarding, fraud checks, invoices and payments. Players attack it through challenge tiers (recon/system-prompt extraction, policy bypass via goal manipulation, data exfiltration, destructive actions, RCE through tool poisoning and MCP). Challenges are detected automatically, offer hints and are mapped to the OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10s and ATLAS. It is attacker-side practice only: there are no walkthroughs and no defence or detection exercises, and multi-agent and memory-poisoning challenges are still on the roadmap.

courses.title: ATLAS (v2026.08)
courses.description: A knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, mitigations and case studies against AI systems (16 tactics and 84 techniques as of v5.1, Nov 2025). Releases from Dec 2025 to Sep 2026 add many agent techniques: AI agent tool poisoning, supply-chain rug pull, local AI agent compromise, agent configuration discovery, escape to host and deepfake-assisted phishing. New case studies include poisoned MCP servers, EchoLeak and computer-use agent hijacking. It is a reference, not a course; the website is JavaScript-rendered, so content was checked through the release notes.

courses.title: AI RMF 1.0 + Playbook + GenAI Profile (AI 600-1)
courses.description: A voluntary risk-management framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) with a companion playbook. The GenAI Profile defines 12 GenAI risks, including confabulation, data privacy, human-AI configuration (automation bias), information security (prompt injection, AI-enabled phishing), intellectual property and value chain, and gives hundreds of suggested actions tagged by function, among them AI inventory, go/no-go thresholds, supplier assessments and incident disclosure. Agents appear only in passing. It is reading only.

courses.title: AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial ML Taxonomy
courses.description: A technical taxonomy of adversarial ML attacks and mitigations. The predictive AI part covers evasion, poisoning and privacy/extraction; the generative AI part covers supply chain attacks, direct prompting attacks, indirect prompt injection, a short section on agent security, and benchmarks. A final chapter discusses key challenges and the limits of mitigations. It is research-grade reading with no exercises.

Reviewed syllabus: A draft NIST CSF 2.0 community profile organised around three focus areas: Secure (AI system components and supply chain), Defend (AI-enabled cyber defence such as alert triage, incident response and agent swarms) and Thwart (AI-enabled attacks such as deepfake spear-phishing, AI-generated malware and autonomous attack agents). courses.title: NICE Framework — AI Security competency area (NF-COM-002)
courses.description: A competency-area definition in the NICE workforce framework. In v2.1.0 (Dec 2025) it received an updated description and, for the first time, 70 knowledge and 20 skill statements, covering understanding AI systems and using and securing them. The individual statements could not be viewed. It is a workforce taxonomy for designing roles and training, not learning content, and it does not mention AI agents or supervision.

courses.title: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services
courses.description: Joint Five Eyes guidance (ASD ACSC, CISA, NSA, Canadian Cyber Centre, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK) that defines agentic AI and its components and sets out five risk categories: privilege, design and configuration, behavioural, structural and accountability. It gives best practices across design, development, deployment and operation, for example distinct cryptographic agent identity, a centralised policy decision point, JIT credentials, logs agents cannot write to, human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions, and graduated autonomy with rollback. An appendix lists prerequisites. It is reading only.

N5.8.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: Joint Five Eyes guidance (ASD ACSC, CISA, NSA, Canadian Cyber Centre, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK) that defines agentic AI and its components and sets out five risk categories: privilege, design and configuration, behavioural, structural and accountability. It gives best practices across design, development, deployment and operation, for example distinct cryptographic agent identity, a centralised policy decision point, JIT credentials, logs agents cannot write to, human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions, and graduated autonomy with rollback. An appendix lists prerequisites. It is reading only.

courses.title: Guidelines for Secure AI System Development
courses.description: High-level secure-by-design principles for AI system providers, organised in four lifecycle stages: secure design (staff awareness, threat modelling, system design, model selection), development (supply chain, documentation, technical debt), deployment (infrastructure, incident management, responsible release) and operation (logging and monitoring, updates, information sharing). It predates agents and does not name prompt injection. It is reading only.

courses.title: AI Coding Assistants
courses.description: Joint ANSSI/BSI report on the opportunities and risks of AI coding assistants, aimed at managers and developers. As summarised, it covers hallucinated packages, indirect prompt injection, data and model poisoning, and leakage of code to cloud services. It recommends risk analysis, data and library policies, local hosting, developer training and critical review of suggestions. The full PDF could not be retrieved (proxy blocked bsi.bund.de), so scores rely on the agency page and a press summary.

courses.title: Guidelines & Companion Guide on Securing AI Systems
courses.description: Singapore CSA guidelines with a community-built companion guide that maps security controls to five lifecycle stages (planning, development, deployment, operations, end of life). It starts from risk assessment (MITRE ATLAS, OWASP, STRIDE) and covers supply chain, model and data protection, input and output monitoring, and incident management. It includes a worked LLM chatbot case, a facial-recognition case and a list of AI testing tools. It predates agents.

courses.title: Securing Agentic AI — Addendum
courses.description: Singapore CSA's final addendum on agentic AI. It explains agent components, architectures and autonomy levels, then sets out risk assessment (workflow mapping, taint tracing, the OWASP agentic threats) and lifecycle controls: non-human identity, least privilege, sandboxing, guardrails, logging to SIEM, red teaming and human-in-the-loop. It works through three case studies (SaaS web development, client onboarding, fraud detection) and has annexes on MCP and A2A. It is reading only.

courses.title: Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide
courses.description: CSA guide giving test requirements and actionable red-team steps for 12 agentic threat categories: authorisation and control hijacking, checker-out-of-the-loop, critical system interaction, goal manipulation, hallucination exploitation, blast radius, knowledge-base poisoning, memory manipulation, multi-agent exploitation, resource exhaustion, supply chain and untraceability. Secondary sources mention a tooling table and effectiveness metrics. The full PDF sits behind a download form and was not read; the category structure comes from the CSA page and secondary summaries.

courses.title: Levels of Autonomy for agentic AI (L0–L5)
courses.description: Blog post by the CSA CEO proposing six autonomy levels for agentic AI (L0 no autonomy to L5 self-directed), modelled on SAE J3016. For each level it describes the human role, the controls required, who authorises it and how often it is reviewed, and it argues that autonomy boundaries must be enforced technically. It is a discussion proposal with open questions, not a standard.

courses.title: AI impact index for the 147 SFIA 9 skills (prototype)
courses.description: Prototype index from the SFIA 10 consultation that states, for each SFIA 9 skill, where AI can help, why AI output alone does not evidence the skill, what people remain responsible for, and how this shifts by responsibility level. courses.title: Gandalf / Gandalf: Agent Breaker
courses.description: Browser game in which players attack AI apps. The original Gandalf has players talk a model into revealing a password. courses.title: Web Security Academy — Web LLM attacks
courses.description: Free learning topic plus interactive labs on attacking web apps that integrate LLMs. It covers prompt injection, mapping and exploiting LLM APIs, functions and plugins (excessive agency), chaining vulnerabilities, insecure output handling, indirect prompt injection, training data poisoning, sensitive data leakage, AI-powered scanner attacks (exfiltration, routing-based SSRF) and defences. Labs include indirect prompt injection that deletes a user account; the full lab list and difficulty levels were not displayed.
